question: Does thinking + testing candidate solutions beat thinking alone, and has this been tried and shown to work?

brief.note: Bounded: 5 threads, evidence = benchmark papers and ablations; scope in: LLM inference-time compute, best-of-N with verifiers, SWE agents; out: classical search, non-LLM ensembles.

landscape.note: Landscape: two camps (sampling+verifier scaling vs self-correction failure), one disputed term (verifier quality), key numbers found.

plan.note: Plan: Q1/Q3 via sampling-scaling literature, Q2 via self-correction failure papers, Q4 via Goodhart/overoptimization, Q5 via inference-compute scaling.

depth.note: Depth: read Large Language Monkeys and SWE-Gym in full; quotes captured for C1,C2,C8,C9.

midpoint.note: Midpoint: Q1/Q3 supported (sampling works with sound verifier, saturates with weak one), Q2 supported (self-correction degrades), Q4 supported (overthinking/Goodhart), Q5 partly covered. Remaining work worth it: one edge check on selection failures.

edges.note: Edges: checked selection-failure and multi-agent-tournament literature; no evidence found that a design tournament beats single-shot on tasks where verification is weak, which is the boundary condition.

verify.note: Verify: every claim has a primary source and an exact quote; the single secondary (S6) is not load-bearing on its own.

report.note: Redteam: conclusion would be falsified by a controlled study where design tournaments beat single-shot at equal budget with a sound partial verifier; no such study found. Omitted sources: Verification Trap (snippet only), industrial blog posts.

redteam.note: Would bet on it: the conclusion is conditional on verifier soundness and is supported by three independent primary sources with measured numbers.

subquestions.text: Does test-time search / sample-and-select beat single-attempt reasoning
subquestions.evidence: head-to-head benchmark numbers where the same model with more attempts outperforms one attempt at equal token budget
studies showing self-check, self-consistency or self-critique helping vs hurting

subquestions.text: What evidence exists that multi-candidate tournaments help software engineering agents
subquestions.evidence: SWE-bench or similar with best-of-N, verifier-based selection, or design tournaments
overfitting to a flawed verifier, selection bias, reward hacking, pass@k vs pass@1 confusion

subquestions.text: What do scaling/RL results say about inference-time compute
subquestions.evidence: whether extra sampling plus verification converts into capability at a fixed model

sources.title: Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym
Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
Reward Hacking in the Era of Large Models (survey citing overoptimization)
When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling
Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams

claims.statement: With 16 rollouts and a trained verifier, SWE-Gym reports 32.0% Best@k versus 42.8% Pass@k, so verifier selection recovers only part of the headroom that extra samples create.
claims.quote: With 16 rollouts, the Best@k strategy achieves 32.0% resolve rate compared to 42.8% for Pass@k

claims.statement: Verifier-based selection improves steadily with more rollouts: 20.6 at 1 rollout to 29.8 at 8 and 32.0 at 16.
claims.quote: improving from a resolution rate of 20.6@1 to 29.8@8, and up to 32.0@16

claims.statement: Without external feedback, LLM self-correction can degrade reasoning performance rather than improve it.
claims.quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction

claims.statement: Repeated sampling raises coverage along an exponentiated power law, but in domains without an automatic verifier the common verification approaches plateau, so extra samples stop converting into solved problems.
claims.quote: In domains without automatic verifiers, we show that common approaches to verification plateau

claims.statement: AlphaCode's gains came chiefly from large-scale sampling followed by execution-based filtering, which removed more than 99 percent of samples.
claims.quote: Example tests help us filter out more than 99% of model samples

claims.statement: Best-of-N selection with a learned verifier over-optimizes: its proxy score keeps rising while realised reward peaks and then collapses as N grows.
claims.quote: Selection by the learned verifier inflates its own proxy score (dashed) while realized gold reward peaks near N=512 and falls to 0.10 at N=2048

claims.statement: Optimising an imperfect proxy beyond a critical point decreases performance on the true objective, so a selection rule that is only approximately right has a ceiling.
claims.quote: increasing optimisation of an imperfect proxy beyond some critical point decreases performance on the true objective

claims.statement: Repeated sampling on SWE-bench Lite raised the solved fraction from 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250 samples, above the single-sample state of the art of 43%.
claims.quote: the fraction of issues solved with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct increases from 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250 samples, outperforming the single-sample state-of-the-art of 43%

claims.statement: The benefit of extra attempts depends on the verifier: where answers can be automatically verified, coverage gains translate into performance; where they cannot, majority voting and reward models plateau after several hundred samples.
claims.quote: In domains like coding and formal proofs, where answers can be automatically verified, these increases in coverage directly translate into improved performance.

claims.statement: More inference compute has diminishing marginal returns and can actively hurt: extended reasoning is associated with abandoning previously correct answers, and the optimal amount of thinking varies with problem difficulty.
claims.quote: models exhibit “overthinking”, where extended reasoning is associated with abandoning previously correct answers

claims.statement: With a scorer for every attempt, best-of-N saturates quickly and a single large collaborating team stops improving as it grows; parallel small teams beat both at equal budget.
claims.quote: Best-of-$ sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. One large team of collaborating agents can score higher but stops improving as it grows.

claims.statement: Reward-free selection signals can scale with sample count where self-consistency stalls: self-certainty is reported to scale effectively with N, complement chain-of-thought and generalise to open-ended tasks.
claims.quote: self-certainty (1) scales effectively with increasing sample size N, akin to reward models but without the computational overhead; (2) complements chain-of-thought, improving reasoning performance beyond greedy decoding; and (3) generalizes to open-ended tasks where traditional self-consistency methods fall short
